title: A Genetic Algorithm for Navigating Synthesizable Molecular Spaces
claim: A simple evolutionary loop of crossover, mutation and selection acts directly on composable building units, so every candidate stays valid by construction.
layout: 2 rows; top inputs, bottom left-to-right operators into population loop; boxed operators
description: The top row defines the ingredients: grey synthesis trees (hexagon root, circle reaction nodes, square building-block leaves), three example building-block molecules drawn as chemical structures, and a reaction template with an arrow showing reactants becoming a triazole product. Below, a large rounded box holds the genetic algorithm operators. Crossover on the left combines two parent trees, shown with blue and green subtrees, into a child tree with arrows between steps. Mutation on the right shows four variants (Grow, Shrink, Rerun, Change), with changed nodes in red and white asterisks. A thick arrow leads from the box to a database icon labelled Population, which holds small trees. A return arrow closes the loop and Selection is labelled above it. Red and blue highlights draw the eye first.
caption: A graphical overview of \ours{}, which operates over synthesis trees built from building blocks (squares) and reaction templates (circles). Example blocks and a reaction are drawn above using SmilesDrawer [ref].
abstract: Inspired by the effectiveness of genetic algorithms and the importance of synthesizability in molecular design, we present SynGA, a simple genetic algorithm that operates directly over synthesis routes. Our method features custom crossover and mutation operators that explicitly constrain it to synthesizable molecular space. By modifying the fitness function, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SynGA on a variety of design tasks, including synthesizable analog search and sample-efficient property optimization, for both 2D and 3D objectives. Furthermore, by coupling SynGA with a machine learning-based filter that focuses the building block set, we boost SynGA to state-of-the-art performance. For property optimization, this manifests as a model-based variant SynGBO, which employs SynGA and block filtering in the inner loop of Bayesian optimization. Since SynGA is lightweight and enforces synthesizability by construction, our hope is that SynGA can not only serve as a strong standalone baseline but also as a versatile module that can be incorporated into larger synthesis-aware workflows in the future.
